planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in full sun, well-drained soil; because bloom is very early in the season, site trees away from low-lying frost pockets to protect the flowers that set the nut crop.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, since almonds are highly intolerant of wet feet and poorly drained sites lead to root rot. All-in-One is a genetic dwarf almond selected in California for reliable self-fertility, so unlike most almond varieties it does not need a separate pollinizer tree to set a crop, making it a practical choice for smaller home gardens with room for only one tree. The compact, naturally semi-dwarf habit stays smaller than standard almond trees while still producing a full-size, sweet, flavorful kernel. Very early spring bloom is both a strength and a risk: it allows an early start to the growing season but also exposes flowers to occasional late frost damage, so avoid planting in frost pockets. Harvest in late summer to early fall once the outer hulls split open, then dry nuts thoroughly before storing.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in consistently moist to wet soil in early spring; yellow monkeyflower is a streamside and seep native that needs steady moisture and struggles in average garden soil that dries out between waterings.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil along pond margins, rain gardens, or stream edges in partial shade to full sun, since this species is naturally found growing with its roots at or near the water table. Yellow monkeyflower is a widespread North American wildflower named for the whimsical, grinning face suggested by the dark red spotting inside its bright yellow, snapdragon-like flowers, which bloom over a long season from spring into summer and draw bumblebees and other native pollinators reliably. Plants often behave as short-lived perennials or reseeding annuals, sprawling and rooting at the nodes where stems touch wet soil, which makes them useful as a low, moisture-loving edge planting for water features. Keep the soil from drying out, since this is the single most common cause of failure; in a genuinely wet, boggy spot it needs very little other care.

planting.note: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or plant container-grown stock in spring, into well-drained, average garden soil; peach-leaved bellflower prefers cooler summers and benefits from afternoon shade and reliable moisture in the heat of a Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade in warm climates, or full sun where summers are milder, and keep the shallow, fibrous roots from drying out. Campanula persicifolia is a classic European cottage-garden perennial named for its narrow, willow-like leaves that resemble peach foliage, sending up slender, wiry stems in late spring to early summer topped with a loose spire of large, upward-facing, cup-shaped blue or white flowers that are outstanding as cut flowers. The airy, see-through growth habit makes it a good middle-of-border plant that does not block the view of what is planted behind it. Deadhead spent flower spikes to encourage a possible rebloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in fall or early spring to keep plants vigorous; in hot, humid climates the plant appreciates a bit of afternoon shade and does best treated as a slightly short-lived perennial refreshed periodically from new divisions.

planting.note: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or plant container-grown stock in spring, in lean, sharply drained soil; harebell is adapted to poor, rocky, alkaline soils and struggles in rich, moisture-retentive garden beds, especially through humid Gulf Coast summers.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, gravelly or rocky soil in full sun to light shade, mimicking the exposed, low-fertility sites where this species is found across the Northern Hemisphere in the wild, from Scottish moorland to North American prairie and mountain slopes. Harebell forms a low tuft of rounded basal leaves — the source of its species name — beneath thin, wiry, gracefully arching stems that carry delicate, nodding, bell-shaped blue flowers from early to late summer, a long bloom period for such a diminutive plant. It is exceptionally cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established but is intolerant of soggy soil and heavy, humid heat, making it best suited to a rock garden, gravel bed, or raised trough where drainage is sharp; light afternoon shade helps it cope with hot summer regions. Established clumps spread slowly by rhizome and self-seed lightly without becoming aggressive.
